cards.#1: Malbon put Torrey Pines across the front of a white crown and ran a navy rope over it, and that is the whole design. Nothing on it is loud, which is Malbon at their most restrained and the register in which they are best. Forty-eight dollars, and a course hat you can wear at courses you have never played.
cards.#2: Sunday Golf make the plainest good version of this shape: a white rope crown, black script, nothing else competing for the front. Thirty-five dollars puts it at the bottom end of the category without looking like it does. Reach for it on the days the rest of the outfit is doing the talking.
cards.#3: The Signature comes in loden with gold, a quieter pairing than most rope hats manage. Field Day photograph every hat on a wooden stand rather than a model, which is a small thing that makes their whole catalogue look considered. Forty-five dollars.
cards.#4: Seamus build this on a green rope crown with a stitched leather patch on the front, and the patch is no accident from a shop that forges metal for a living. It is the best-made hat in the group at forty-eight dollars.
cards.#5: Pins & Aces put a pheasant on a cream crown and perforated the crown throughout, so it moves air in a way most rope hats do not. Forty dollars, and they have fourteen photographs of it on their own site if you want to be certain about the bird.
cards.#6: Eastside Golf keep this one to a green rope crown and a circle patch, which is the cleanest shape they make. The branding is there without shouting, so it goes with more than the rest of their catalogue does. Forty-five dollars.
cards.#7: The Rhino Pills trucker runs a mesh back and costs thirty dollars, which makes it the cheapest hat in the run by some distance. Mesh is the correct answer to August, and the graphic carries it past being a plain trucker. Most of Radry’s catalogue is sold out, so this one moves quickly.
cards.#8: Sunday cut this trucker in brown and white with a mesh back, and a mesh back breathes better than anything else in the category. Thirty-five dollars, and it reads as a designed hat rather than a tournament giveaway.
cards.#9: Ghost perforate the crown right across, so the hat is built for heat rather than described that way in the copy. Sixty dollars is a real ask for a plain cap, and this is the one that will keep you comfortable through an August eighteen.
cards.#10: Sugarloaf built this five-panel with THE PLAYERS, in light blue with mesh side panels. A five-panel sits lower and lighter than a rope hat and the mesh does the rest, so this is the one you would actually walk eighteen holes in. Forty-five dollars.
cards.#11: Manors make one bucket hat and this is it, cut from recycled fabric with a full brim. The full brim is the point in August, when the back of your neck is the part that pays. Forty-five pounds, in the currency Manors actually charge.
cards.#12: Gumtree cut this in a 70/30 cotton-nylon they say is water and stain repellent, with a wide brim and a neck flap off the back. Nothing else here covers as much of you. Sixty-five Australian dollars.
cards.#13: Inkwash blue camo covers the whole hat, which puts it closer to the Malbon you reach for in August than the Malbon you photograph. A print this busy hides everything a long afternoon does to a bucket hat. Sixty-eight dollars.
cards.#14: Public Drip cut this bucket in white nylon rather than canvas, which matters when it is a hundred degrees and you are sweating into it. The script P does the rest of the work. Fifty dollars.
cards.#15: The Course Cap is Manors at their plainest and their best: white, a small checker tab, nothing else on it. Thirty-five pounds, and the cap to keep in the car for the rounds you did not plan.
cards.#16: Cream cotton carries a Negroni-orange Italian script across the front, and Gumtree are Australian, so the joke is deliberate. Cream and orange is a summer palette rather than a golf one, and it reads from a distance. Fifty-five Australian dollars for the least serious hat in the group.
cards.#17: Radry put an orange flame script on a green crown and get away with it, which most brands their size cannot do. Green and orange should not work together on a golf cap and here they do. Thirty-five dollars.
cards.#18: Macade choose colour better than almost anyone making golf clothing, and this jade snapback is the proof. Jade is a shade most brands leave alone, and on a plain snapback it does all the work. Forty-five pounds, in the currency they actually charge.
cards.#19: Field Day cut this as a two-tone caddie cap for the Western Golf Association, whose Evans Scholars programme sends caddies to college. It is a caddie cap in name and in shape, and the two-tone keeps it from reading as a costume. Fifty-nine dollars.
cards.#20: Fella put ALL GEAR NO GAME across a teal crown with contrast stitching, and the text does the rest of the work. Teal and contrast stitching would be plenty on their own, but the line is the reason you buy it. Fifty dollars, and they know exactly what they are.
cards.#21: Huega House stack San Diego and 2022 under a cream collegiate script on a brown crown, which is the cleanest thing they make. Collegiate lettering on brown reads as a school hat rather than a golf one. Forty-five dollars.
cards.#22: Siegelman put their horse on a cream crown with an olive brim, and it is the most wearable and least shouty thing they make. Cream and olive is the summer half of their palette and the half that goes with everything. Seventy-six dollars is a Siegelman price.
cards.#23: Devereux run a black and white pinstripe across this one, which almost nobody does on a golf cap. The stripe reads as texture from any distance, and thirty-eight dollars is a fair number for it.
cards.#24: Students keep this one black and white and structured, which makes it their cleanest snapback. Fifty dollars, and the structure means it holds its shape instead of folding at the front.
cards.#25: Random Golf Club put a shield patch on a green crown and charge twenty dollars for it, which makes it the cheapest good hat in the group. Nothing about it reads as a twenty dollar cap.
cards.#26: Matchstick run a PNW script across a navy dad hat, and the same catalogue produced a Goonies ball marker, which tells you the register they work in. Navy and an unstructured crown make it the plainest thing they sell. Forty dollars.
cards.#27: Blue, red and yellow panels make this the loudest hat in the group, and Birds of Condor being Australian explains most of it. The panels break the crown up so no single colour has to carry it. Sixty Australian dollars, and a relief among all the navy.
cards.#28: Olydoe put a red shield on a cream crown and left it there. The shield is small enough to read as a detail rather than a logo, which is most of why the hat works. Forty-five dollars, priced like a brand that is not trying to make a point with the number.

kickers.1: A rope across the front of an unstructured crown is the shape that says golf without saying much else. Most of these are cotton twill and most sit low. Two are perforated as well, which is the difference between a hat for nine holes and one for eighteen.
kickers.2: Trucker backs, perforated crowns and mesh side panels do the work in August, and this is the category that gets the least attention for it. Radry’s trucker is thirty dollars, the cheapest hat in the run.
kickers.3: Four buckets follow, and one of them carries a neck flap. If you have played Lions or Hancock at two in the afternoon in July, you already understand the case for a full brim.
kickers.4: These are cotton twill in five panels, structured and unstructured, with nothing technical and nothing claiming to wick. They are the caps you keep in the car for the round you did not plan.
